claims.claim: People with Alzheimer's disease can still improve a movement skill through repeated practice (implicit or procedural learning), even without being aware of learning it, though their performance stays below that of people without dementia.
claims.supporting_passage: "The present review discusses 23 experimental studies on implicit motor-skill learning in patients with Alzheimer's disease (AD). All studies found intact implicit motor-learning capacities." (Abstract) ... "In implicit learning, skills are mastered without awareness, often simply by repeated exposure, and can be unconsciously revived from implicit memory" (Introduction) ... "All the studies found preserved motor-skill learning in AD patients although their overall performance levels in terms of reaction and movement time were always inferior to those of the controls." ... "Patients are capable of acquiring motor skills without awareness simply by repeated exposure, although their performances will not reach normal levels." (Conclusions)
claims.location: Abstract; full text Introduction, Performance and Amount of Learning, Conclusions and Recommendations
claims.pico_timeframe: People with clinically diagnosed Alzheimer's disease (mostly mild) versus healthy controls in 23 laboratory studies published 1985 to 2005; exposure repeated practice of procedural motor tasks (maze, rotor pursuit, serial reaction time, mirror tracing, puzzle assembly); outcome speed or error change within sessions.
claims.safe_wording: A person with Alzheimer's disease who does not remember yesterday's practice may still have learned from it. A 2007 review of 23 laboratory studies found that people with Alzheimer's disease still got better at movement tasks with repeated practice, even though they stayed slower than people without dementia.
claims.qualifications: Laboratory tasks, not real rehabilitation tasks; mainly mild Alzheimer's disease; people who could not do a task were removed from the analyses; learning did not reach normal levels and transferred little to other skills. Say 'often relatively preserved', not 'intact' or 'normal'. Do not extend to other dementias.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Palma 2023 scoping review (PMID:37337358): 7 of 15 studies reported that cognitive impairment impaired motor learning, though most were at high risk of bias. The 2007 review itself notes weaker learning on some tasks (maze without vision; spatial sequence tasks) and in 'mildly' versus 'very mildly' demented groups in one study.

numbers.meaning: experimental studies in the review, published 1985 to 2005

claims.claim: The review recommends frequent, consistent practice of the same movement, in a setting and with equipment like those the person uses in daily life, avoiding doing two things at once, and good vision; it found no Alzheimer's studies testing demonstration.
claims.supporting_passage: "The studies we reviewed showed that in (re)learning motor skills, constant, or rather frequent and consistent practice is important in AD patients. This way of learning draws less on episodic memory and other cognitive functions compromised in AD patients. These data also suggest that practice under dual-task conditions should also be avoided." ... "Because AD patients have difficulty in generalizing the motor skills learned during the sessions, training has to take place in an environment that closely resembles the one in which the skill is going to be used and presumably with tools used by the AD patient in his or her daily life." ... "Patients with AD appear to remain dependent upon visual feedback throughout training and performance. Screening and subsequent correction of visual problems or the use of visual aids can be effective in the training process in this group" ... On guidance, observation and mental practice: "Our automated computer search and an extra search combining the three keywords with Alzheimer dementia both failed to generate any relevant studies that employed one of these training methods." ... On verbal feedback: "it may be hypothesized that both forms of feedback knowledge probably place too much weight on the cognitive abilities in AD patients and therefore contribute little to successful performance."
claims.location: Full text: Conclusions and Recommendations; Practice; Feedback
claims.pico_timeframe: Recommendations inferred by the authors from laboratory studies in Alzheimer's disease (constant versus random practice; visual feedback).
claims.safe_wording: Practise the same movement the same way each time, in the place and with the chair, frame or bed the person will actually use, one task at a time, with glasses on. A review of the research recommends consistent practice of this kind for people with Alzheimer's disease because it relies less on remembering the session.
claims.qualifications: These are the review authors' recommendations drawn from laboratory studies, not tested rehabilitation trials. 'Show rather than tell' and 'use few words' were not tested in Alzheimer's disease (the review found no studies of demonstration and only hypothesised that verbal feedback helps little); present them as practical suggestions, not findings. The judge's 'same sit-to-stand sequence with one cue each time' fits the consistent-practice recommendation; 'one cue' is judgement.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: No trial in this batch compared consistent practice with other methods in real rehabilitation for people with dementia.

claims.claim: In a randomised trial, dementia-adapted strength and function training improved strength and chair-stand performance in people with mild to moderate dementia, and the degree of cognitive impairment did not predict who benefited.
claims.supporting_passage: "Individuals with confirmed mild to moderate dementia, no severe somatic or psychological disease, and ability to walk 10 m." ... "Supervised, progressive resistance and functional group training for 3 months specifically developed for people with dementia (intervention, n = 62) compared with a low-intensity motor placebo activity (control, n = 60)." ... "Training significantly improved both primary outcomes" ... "Training gains were partly sustained during follow-up. Low baseline performance on motor tasks but not cognitive impairment predicted positive training response." ... "The intensive, dementia-adjusted training was feasible and substantially improved motor performance in frail, older people with dementia"
claims.pico_timeframe: 122 people with mild to moderate dementia able to walk 10 m, outpatient geriatric rehabilitation, Germany, 2006 to 2009 / 3 months of supervised progressive resistance and functional group training adapted for dementia / low-intensity motor placebo activity / leg-press maximal strength and five-chair-stand time / 3 months, with 3-month follow-up.
claims.safe_wording: In a German trial of 122 people with mild to moderate dementia, 3 months of supervised strength and balance training designed for people with dementia made them stronger and quicker at standing up from a chair than gentle placebo exercise. How much their memory and thinking were affected did not predict who improved; people who started weakest gained most.
claims.qualifications: Participants could walk 10 m and had no severe illness; gains were only partly kept 3 months after training stopped. Do not quote the strength percentages (the abstract's units are inconsistent).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Single trial; the Cochrane review of rehabilitation after hip fracture for people with dementia (Smith 2020, PMID 32031676, abstract seen, not added as a source) rated most evidence very low certainty, so do not generalise to all rehabilitation settings.

numbers.meaning: people randomised (62 training, 60 placebo activity)
training period, followed by 3 months without training

claims.claim: Many people with dementia receive no rehabilitation after hip fracture surgery.
claims.supporting_passage: "Of 11,200 individuals with dementia who experienced a hip fracture during the study period, 4,494 (40.1%) received no rehabilitation, 2,474 (22.1%) were admitted to CCC, 1,157 (10.3%) received HCR, and 3,075 (27.4%) received IPR." ... "Postfracture rehabilitation for older adults with dementia is associated with lower risk of LTC placement and mortality. Improving access to rehabilitation services for this vulnerable population may improve postfracture outcomes."
claims.pico_timeframe: Community-dwelling adults with dementia having hip fracture surgery, Ontario, Canada, 2003 to 2011 / type of post-fracture rehabilitation received / outcomes: care home placement, mortality, falls, repeat fracture.
claims.safe_wording: In Ontario, Canada, about 4 in 10 people with dementia living at home who had surgery for a hip fracture between 2003 and 2011 got no rehabilitation afterwards.
claims.qualifications: Canadian data from 2003 to 2011. The abstract gives no figure for people without dementia and no reasons, so do not say they were 'excluded because of dementia'. The lower care home placement and death rates with rehabilitation are associations; fitter people may have been chosen for rehabilitation.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: No UK access figure was verified in this batch (no National Audit of Intermediate Care report could be opened).

numbers.meaning: people with dementia receiving no rehabilitation after hip fracture surgery, Ontario 2003 to 2011; say 'about 4 in 10'

claims.claim: The evidence on preserved motor learning comes mainly from laboratory tasks in Alzheimer's disease; transfer to everyday tasks and to other dementias is less certain, and some studies find learning is impaired.
claims.supporting_passage: van Halteren 2007: "It should be noted that in all studies the patients that could not perform the task were eliminated from the analyses." ... "Clearly, AD patients show preserved implicit learning abilities that can be utilized in teaching (motor) skills, yet transfer to other skills is minimal." Palma 2023: "we selected 15 studies describing cognitive assessment tools, experimental designs, and the severity of cognitive impairment. Although seven studies reported that cognitive impairment impaired motor learning, most studies included a high risk of bias."
claims.location: van Halteren full text (Implicit Learning Ability; Conclusions); Palma abstract
claims.pico_timeframe: Older adults with Alzheimer's disease or mild cognitive impairment in motor learning experiments.
claims.safe_wording: Most of this research used laboratory tasks with people with Alzheimer's disease. Some studies find learning is weaker, and it is less clear for other types of dementia.
claims.qualifications: State the limitation once, plainly.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: See C02-21-a.

numbers.meaning: studies in the 2023 scoping review that reported impaired motor learning with cognitive impairment (most at high risk of bias)

claims.claim: Observational research by Baltes and colleagues described a pattern in which dependent behaviour of older people was met with help while independent behaviour was ignored or met with more help, in institutions and at home.
claims.supporting_passage: Baltes 1994: "Research has attested to the prevalence of a "dependency-support" and "independence-ignore" script characterizing the interactions between staff and elderly residents in long-term care institutions." Baltes and Wahl 1992: "This study tested the generalizability of the dependency-support script, a behavioral system describing and explaining dependent behaviors of the institutionalized elderly. A comparative study with 22 community-dwelling elderly was conducted, which identified typical interaction patterns between the elderly and family members or home health nurses. The dominant interaction pattern in the community setting, too, was the dependency-support script." ... "Independent behaviors were followed about twice as often by an incongruent (dependence-supportive) than by a congruent (independence-supportive) response."
claims.pico_timeframe: Older people in German long-term care institutions and (1992) 22 older people at home with family or home nurses / observed sequences of behaviour and response / no outcome on long-term ability.
claims.safe_wording: Researchers in Berlin, publishing in the early 1990s, watched how staff responded to older people in long-term care. When a resident needed help, staff paid attention and helped. When a resident managed alone, it tended to go unnoticed. A 1992 study of 22 older people at home found the same: when they did something for themselves, family or nurses were about twice as likely to step in and help as to encourage them.
claims.qualifications: Small, old German studies; observational; describe responses, not long-term loss of ability. The 1994 abstract cites the institutional research without dates, so say 'published in the early 1990s' rather than naming a decade of fieldwork.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: No modern UK observational replication was checked.

numbers.meaning: older people living at home in the 1992 study
independent actions followed by dependence-supportive rather than independence-supportive responses (1992 study, at home)

claims.claim: A staff training programme in 3 institutions reduced dependence-supportive staff behaviour, increased independence-supportive behaviour and increased residents' independent self-care behaviour.
claims.supporting_passage: "To examine whether the scripts could be modified, a staff training program (focusing on communication skills, knowledge about aging, and basic behavior principles) was implemented in 3 different institutions. Observational data on staff-resident interactions in the context of self-care were collected pre- and postintervention. Findings revealed significant changes for the experimental group. Specifically, a decrease in dependence-supportive behavior of staff and an increase in their independence-supportive behavior, an increase in independent behavior of residents, and an increase in independence-related interaction patterns were demonstrated."
claims.pico_timeframe: Staff and residents in 3 German long-term care institutions / staff training in communication, ageing and behaviour principles / comparison group (details not in abstract) / observed staff and resident behaviour during self-care, before and after training / follow-up length not stated.
claims.safe_wording: In a 1994 German study, staff in 3 care institutions were trained in communication, ageing and simple behaviour principles. Afterwards, staff did less for residents and encouraged them more, and residents did more of their own self-care.
claims.qualifications: Sample size, how groups were formed and how long the change lasted are not in the abstract; the outcome was observed behaviour during self-care, not a measured gain in function. Date and place the study.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: A 2024 Dutch trial (C02-14-d) changed staff behaviour but did not show a significant change in residents' self-reliance.

numbers.meaning: institutions where the training was delivered

claims.claim: Function-focused (restorative) care has been tested in randomised trials in nursing homes; in a 12-home US trial it improved mobility, walking, bathing and stair climbing.
claims.supporting_passage: "A randomized controlled repeated-measure design was used, and generalized estimating equations were used to evaluate status at baseline and 4 and 12 months after initiation of the Res-Care intervention." ... "Twelve nursing homes in Maryland." ... "Four hundred eighty-seven residents consented and were eligible" ... "Res-Care was a two-tiered self-efficacy-based intervention focused on motivating nursing assistants and residents to engage in functional and physical activities." ... "Significant treatment-by-time interactions (P<.05) were found for the Tinetti Mobility Score and its gait and balance subscores and for walking, bathing, and stair climbing." ... "The findings provide some evidence for the utility and safety of a Res-Care intervention in terms of improving function in NH residents."
claims.pico_timeframe: 487 nursing home residents (mean age 83.8, mean MMSE 20.4), 12 Maryland nursing homes / programme motivating nursing assistants and residents to do functional and physical activity / control homes / Barthel items, Tinetti gait and balance, strength, quality of life / 4 and 12 months.
claims.safe_wording: In a US trial in 12 nursing homes, training care assistants to encourage residents to do what they could for themselves improved residents' walking, balance, bathing and stair climbing over a year, compared with homes without the programme.
claims.qualifications: The abstract gives no effect sizes; authors call it 'some evidence'. US nursing homes, 2009.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Vluggen 2024 (C02-14-d) did not show a significant resident benefit.

numbers.meaning: nursing homes in the trial
residents

claims.claim: A recent Dutch cluster-randomised trial of a staff programme improved nurses' encouragement of residents' independence but did not show a statistically significant change in residents' self-reliance.
claims.supporting_passage: "Twenty-eight nursing home wards, with 287 nurses and 241 residents participated in the study. A statistically significant treatment by time interaction effect was observed in nurses' activity encouragement behavior at three months (d = 0.53; p = .003; 95 % CI 1.88-8.02) and at nine months (d = 0.38; p = .02; 95 % CI 0.67-7.27). No statistically significant treatment by time interaction effects were observed in residents' self-reliance in activities of daily living. However, a trend was observed towards a less pronounced decrease in self-reliance in those residents allocated to wards that exposed nurses to the SELF-program"
claims.pico_timeframe: 28 Dutch nursing home wards, 287 nurses, 241 residents / SELF-program (7 interactive training sessions over 3 months, per conference abstract seen in Consensus) / care as usual / nurses' activity encouragement (MAINtAIN), residents' self-reliance in daily activities (GARS-4) / 6 months (residents), 9 months (nurses).
claims.safe_wording: In a Dutch trial in 28 nursing home wards, training helped nurses encourage residents to do more for themselves. Residents' independence in daily activities did not change clearly over 6 months, though it declined a little less on trained wards.
claims.qualifications: State both halves. 'Did not change clearly' is the correct reading of p = .07, not 'no effect'.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Contrasts with Res-Care 2009 and Baltes 1994. The trial's own background notes that such programmes 'have demonstrated inconsistent effects'.

numbers.meaning: trial size, the Netherlands, recruitment from 2021

claims.claim: Time pressure and staff shortages are reasons staff give for still taking over tasks residents could do themselves.
claims.supporting_passage: "Still, time constraints, staffing shortages and lack of motivation were put forwards as factors leading some nurses to still take over tasks." ... "Contextual barriers to program implementation and outcomes included staffing shortages, low program attendance, time constraints, lack of manager support, and delivery of the program during the COVID-19 pandemic."
claims.pico_timeframe: Nurses and trainers on 28 Dutch nursing home wards during a 9-month trial; checklists, logbooks, questionnaires and focus groups.
claims.safe_wording: In the Dutch trial, nurses named time pressure and staff shortages among the reasons some of them still took over tasks that residents could do themselves.
claims.qualifications: Staff-reported barriers from one Dutch trial, not a measurement of how much extra time supported care takes. The position that time and training must be built into the rota is judgement and should be written as such ('Care homes should...').
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: No study in this batch measured the minutes needed for supported versus done-for care; do not put a time figure on a visual clock.

claims.claim: Reablement aims to maximise independence rather than doing tasks for people; trial evidence on its effects was very low certainty.
claims.supporting_passage: "Unlike traditional home-care services, reablement is frequently time-limited (usually six to 12 weeks) and aims to maximise independence by offering an intensive multidisciplinary, person-centred and goal-directed intervention." ... "We are very uncertain as to the effects of reablement compared with usual care as the evidence was of very low quality for all of the outcomes reported."
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults 65+ receiving home care in Western Australia and Norway / time-limited reablement up to 12 weeks / usual home care / function, mortality, admissions, quality of life / up to 24 months; searches to mid-2015.
claims.safe_wording: Home care 'reablement' services aim to help people do things for themselves again. A 2016 Cochrane review found only 2 trials and was very uncertain about their effects.
claims.qualifications: Optional context; home care, not care homes; searches from 2015 and no update checked.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Newer reablement trials were not reviewed in this batch.

numbers.meaning: evidence base of the 2016 Cochrane review

claims.claim: Doing a task for someone saves time today and can cost them ability later.
claims.supporting_passage: Vluggen 2024 (background, not a finding): "However, nurses often take over tasks unnecessarily, which can deprive resident's remaining abilities."
claims.pico_timeframe: No study in this batch measured long-term loss of ability caused by staff doing tasks for residents.
claims.safe_wording: Present as reasoning, not a finding: 'If staff always do it, residents get less practice. Trials that trained staff to encourage residents found gains in some homes and not in others.'
claims.qualifications: A background sentence in a paper's introduction is not that paper's finding. Do not say doing tasks for people 'causes' or 'leads to' loss of ability.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Mixed trial results (Res-Care versus SELF).

claims.claim: The top of a walking stick should be level with the crease of the wrist when the person stands upright with arms relaxed by their sides.
claims.supporting_passage: "The top of a cane or walker should be the same height as the wrist crease when the patient is standing upright with arms relaxed at his or her sides."
claims.pico_timeframe: Clinical advice for older adults fitting canes and walkers.
claims.safe_wording: Stand up straight in your usual shoes with your arms hanging loosely. The top of the stick should be level with the crease on the inside of your wrist.
claims.qualifications: Professional advice from a clinical review, not a trial. 'In your usual shoes' is a practical addition, not from the source; keep or drop.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Camara 2019 (PMID 31322813, abstract seen, not added as a source) found sticks set longer than wrist height increased postural sway in 18 older women, consistent with the advice.

claims.claim: A stick is held in the hand opposite the weak or painful leg and moved forward at the same time as that leg.
claims.supporting_passage: "A cane should be held contralateral to a weak or painful lower extremity and advanced simultaneously with the contralateral leg."
claims.pico_timeframe: Clinical advice for one-sided leg weakness or pain.
claims.safe_wording: Hold the stick in the hand on the opposite side to the painful or weak leg, and move the stick forward at the same time as that leg.
claims.qualifications: Applies to pain or weakness on one side. Someone with problems in both legs or poor balance may need a different aid (see C02-01-e).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None found.

claims.claim: Among people who use walking sticks, wrong height, poor condition, use in the wrong hand and lack of professional advice are common.
claims.supporting_passage: Sheehan 2008: "Fifty randomly selected patients attending a rheumatology department were surveyed to determine whether their stick was appropriate to their needs and whether they were using it correctly." ... "Of the 50 patients, 38% used their stick incorrectly, usually in the wrong hand. Forty-four per cent of sticks were of the wrong length and 54% were in imperfect condition, the main defect being a worn ferrule." Liu 2011: "Five major problems from data analysis were identified: lack of medical consultation for device selection/use, incorrect cane height/maintenance, placement of cane in improper hand, inability to maintain the proper reciprocal gait pattern, and improper posture during ambulation." Bradley 2011: "Most patients with assistive devices have never been instructed on the proper use and often have devices that are inappropriate, damaged, or are of the incorrect height." George 1988: "Many of the aids that the elderly had were faulty, including half of the walking aids and 15% of hearing aids, reading spectacles, and dentures"
claims.pico_timeframe: Sheehan: 50 stick users with arthritis, rheumatology department, England, 2008 (adults, not only older people). Liu: 93 cane users aged 65+, US senior living communities. George: 140 people over 75, one English general practice, 1988.
claims.safe_wording: In a survey of 50 stick users at an English hospital arthritis clinic, 44 in 100 sticks were the wrong length and 54 in 100 were in poor condition, most often because the rubber tip was worn. About 4 in 10 people were using their stick wrongly, usually in the wrong hand. A US study of 93 stick users aged over 65 found the same problems, and many had never had professional advice when choosing the stick.
claims.qualifications: Small surveys; Sheehan's clinic patients were not all older people. Liu gives no percentages in the abstract, so quote only Sheehan's figures. George 1988 ('half of the walking aids' faulty, 140 people over 75) is dated and 'walking aids' includes frames; use only with the year.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: No recent UK survey of stick fit was found.

numbers.meaning: sticks of the wrong length, 50 stick users, rheumatology department, England, 2008
sticks in imperfect condition, main defect a worn ferrule (same survey)
people using the stick incorrectly, usually in the wrong hand (same survey)
people who had been taught who used their stick correctly (same survey); do not compare with the 50% figure for the untrained, which measured correct hand only
cane users aged 65+ in the US study (no percentages in abstract)
walking aids found faulty among 140 people over 75 in one English practice, 1988

claims.claim: A worn rubber tip (ferrule) is a common defect and should be checked and replaced.
claims.supporting_passage: "Walking sticks are used widely by people with arthritis, principally to reduce pain and improve stability and balance. However, they are frequently used incorrectly and can be dangerous if not properly maintained." ... "54% were in imperfect condition, the main defect being a worn ferrule." ... "These findings highlight the importance of educating patients on how to obtain greatest benefit from their walking stick and of the necessity to check it regularly for defects to ensure safe usage."
claims.pico_timeframe: 50 stick users with arthritis, rheumatology department, England, 2008.
claims.safe_wording: Turn the stick over and look at the rubber tip. A worn tip was the most common defect in one English clinic survey, and the authors advise checking sticks regularly for faults. If the tread is worn smooth, replace the tip.
claims.qualifications: The source says poorly maintained sticks 'can be dangerous' and names the worn ferrule as the main defect; it does not measure grip. Do not claim a worn tip 'grips less well' as a finding. 'Replace it' is practical advice.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: No NHS or physiotherapy leaflet could be opened (web pages blocked; Drive search found none).

claims.claim: The right aid depends on strength, balance and cognition; people with weakness or poor balance may need a frame rather than a stick, and clinicians should check height, fit and maintenance.
claims.supporting_passage: "Selection of a suitable device depends on the patient's strength, endurance, balance, cognitive function, and environmental demands." ... "Walkers improve stability in those with lower extremity weakness or poor balance and facilitate improved mobility by increasing the patient's base of support and supporting the patient's weight. Walkers require greater attentional demands than canes and make using stairs difficult." ... "Clinicians should routinely evaluate their patients' assistive devices to ensure proper height, fit, and maintenance, and also counsel patients on correct use of the device."
claims.pico_timeframe: Clinical advice for older adults choosing assistive devices.
claims.safe_wording: A stick is the wrong aid for some people. If both legs are weak or balance is poor, a walking frame may be safer; ask a physiotherapist or GP to check which aid suits you and that it fits.
claims.qualifications: Clinical review advice. Frames have downsides too (more attention needed, harder on stairs).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None found.

claims.claim: In a randomised trial of 110 frail patients aged 65+ (mean 78) having colorectal cancer surgery within an enhanced recovery pathway, a multimodal programme started before surgery did not reduce 30-day complications compared with the same programme started after surgery.
claims.supporting_passage: "A total of 418 patients 65 years or older were assessed for eligibility. Of these, 298 patients were excluded (not frail [n = 290], unable to exercise [n = 3], and planned neoadjuvant treatment [n = 5]), and 120 frail patients (Fried Frailty Index,≥2) were randomized." ... "Hence, 110 patients were included in the intention-to-treat analysis (55 in the prehabilitation [Prehab] and 55 in the rehabilitation [Rehab] groups)." ... "Multimodal program involving exercise, nutritional, and psychological interventions initiated before (Prehab group) or after (Rehab group) surgery. All patients were treated within a standardized enhanced recovery pathway." ... "Of 110 patients randomized, mean (SD) age was 78 (7) years" ... "There was no between-group difference in the primary outcome measure, 30-day Comprehensive Complications Index (adjusted mean difference, -3.2; 95% CI, -11.8 to 5.3; P = .45)." Discussion (via Scite, the article's own text): "The low adherence of patients to the rehabilitation program (14%), however, supports that this control intervention was closer to a sham condition than to an active comparator." ... "Although our sample size was relatively small (n = 110), the lower bounds of the 95% CI observed for between-group differences in CCI (11.8) suggest that we were unlikely to miss a meaningful benefit of the intervention due to type II error (when accounting for the reported minimal important difference of 10)."
claims.location: Abstract; Discussion (verbatim sentences retrieved through Scite)
claims.pico_timeframe: 110 frail adults 65+ (mean 78), colorectal cancer resection (79% minimally invasive), 2 Montreal hospitals, 2015 to 2019 / 4-week exercise, nutrition and psychological programme before surgery / same programme for 4 weeks after surgery / Comprehensive Complication Index at 30 days.
claims.safe_wording: In a Montreal trial, 110 frail people aged 65 and over (average age 78) having bowel cancer surgery were given a 4-week programme of exercise, nutrition and psychological support. Half started it before the operation; the other half were offered the same programme after it. Complications in the 30 days after surgery did not differ clearly between the two groups. Only about 1 in 7 people in the after-surgery group kept to that programme, so in practice the comparison was close to no programme.
claims.qualifications: Follow the editor: state the comparison with the same programme after surgery; do not write a bare 'gave no fewer complications'. Bowel cancer surgery within a well-run enhanced recovery pathway; the authors note complication rates were similar to unselected patients, so benefit may be smaller where perioperative care is already optimised. The judge's underpowering concern is partly answered by the authors' confidence-interval argument, but 110 is small.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Newer pooled analyses disagree (see C02-24-f). A 2025 meta-analysis reporting a 'high certainty' reduction in complications in frail older people (Xie et al, Arch Gerontol Geriatr, PMID 41518969) is RETRACTED according to Scite (notice dated 1 April 2026; PubMed not yet tagged). Do not cite it.

numbers.meaning: frail patients analysed (55 per group), from 120 randomised
mean age in years
programme length, before surgery (Prehab) or after surgery (Rehab)
adherence to the after-surgery programme in the comparison group; say 'about 1 in 7'
adjusted difference in Comprehensive Complication Index (0 to 100 scale); not for public posts
screened patients excluded as not frail

claims.claim: Secondary outcomes, including recovery of walking capacity, length of stay and readmissions, did not differ between groups.
claims.supporting_passage: "Secondary outcomes were 30-day overall and severe complications, primary and total length of hospital stay, 30-day emergency department visits and hospital readmissions, recovery of walking capacity, and patient-reported outcome measures." ... "Secondary outcome measures were also not different between groups." Discussion (via Scite): "We also did not observe between-group differences in primary and total LOS, rates of readmission and emergency department visits, postoperative walking capacity, and PROMs."
claims.pico_timeframe: As C02-24-a; walking capacity by 6-minute walk test at baseline, before surgery and 4 weeks after surgery.
claims.safe_wording: Walking ability 4 weeks after the operation, time in hospital and readmissions were also similar in the two groups.
claims.qualifications: Say 'did not differ clearly' or 'were similar', not 'had no effect'.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: The umbrella review (C02-24-d) rates functional recovery improvement with any prehabilitation in cancer surgery as moderate certainty across all adults.

claims.claim: The prehabilitation programme lasted about 4 weeks before surgery.
claims.supporting_passage: (via Scite, the article's own text) "Eligible patients were randomly assigned 1:1 to receive a 4-week prehabilitation program (Prehab group) or a 4-week postoperative rehabilitation program (Rehab group)." ... "The program started after the baseline visit and continued for 4 weeks before surgery, as recommended by the Canadian Oncological Society." ... "Patients were asked to attend training sessions supervised by a trained kinesiologist at the hospital prehabilitation unit once a week for 4 weeks." ... "In addition to the supervised exercise sessions, participants were prescribed a personalized home-based program of aerobic activities (walk daily for a total of 30 minutes as moderate-intensity aerobic activity) and resistance training (elastic band routine 3 times per week)" ... Discussion: "Third, a prehabilitation program lasting 4 to 5 weeks may not be sufficient to increase physiological reserve preoperatively and reduce postoperative complications."
claims.location: Methods (Study procedures; Prehabilitation; Exercise intervention) and Discussion, verbatim via Scite
claims.safe_wording: The programme ran for 4 weeks before surgery: one supervised exercise session a week plus daily walking and home strength exercises, with nutrition and psychological support.
claims.qualifications: The authors themselves suggest 4 to 5 weeks may be too short; a longer programme was not tested.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None.

numbers.meaning: planned programme length before surgery
supervised sessions; plus 30 minutes daily walking and elastic band training 3 times a week at home

claims.claim: An umbrella review found low to very low certainty evidence that prehabilitation reduces complications, and moderate certainty evidence that any prehabilitation improves functional recovery after cancer surgery.
claims.supporting_passage: "From 1412 titles, 55 systematic reviews were included. For patients with cancer undergoing surgery who participate in any prehabilitation, moderate certainty evidence supports improvements in functional recovery. Low to very low certainty evidence supports reductions in complications (mixed, cardiovascular, and cancer surgery), non-home discharge (orthopaedic surgery), and length of stay (mixed, cardiovascular, and cancer surgery). There was low to very low certainty evidence that exercise prehabilitation reduces the risk of complications, non-home discharge, and length of stay." ... "Low certainty evidence suggests that prehabilitation may improve postoperative outcomes."
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults of any age having elective surgery; 55 systematic reviews searched to October 2020; GRADE certainty.
claims.safe_wording: A 2022 review of 55 earlier reviews rated the evidence that prehabilitation reduces complications as low or very low certainty. It found moderate certainty that prehabilitation helps people with cancer recover their physical function after surgery.
claims.qualifications: All adults, not frail older people specifically. The moderate-certainty finding is for any prehabilitation in cancer surgery, not exercise alone. Searches end 2020.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: See C02-24-f for later pooled analyses.

numbers.meaning: systematic reviews in the umbrella review

claims.claim: A home-based exercise prehabilitation trial in older people with frailty having cancer surgery did not significantly improve its primary outcome (walking distance).
claims.supporting_passage: "This double blind randomised trial enrolled people ≥60 yr having elective cancer surgery and ≥3 weeks from enrolment to surgery as eligible. Participation in a remotely supported, home-based exercise prehabilitation program plus nutritional guidance was compared with standard care plus written advice on age-appropriate activity and nutrition. The primary outcome was 6-min walk test (6MWT) distance at the first postoperative clinic visit." ... "Of 543 patients assessed, 254 were eligible and 204 (80%) were randomised (102 per arm); 182 (94 intervention and 88 control) had surgery and were analysed. Mean age was 74 yr and 57% were female. Mean duration of participation was 5 weeks, mean adherence was 61% (range 0%-100%). We found no significant difference in 6MWT at follow-up (+14 m, 95% confidence interval -26-55 m, P=0.486), or for secondary outcomes. Analyses using a prespecified adherence definition of ≥80% supported improvements in 6MWT distance, complication count, and disability."
claims.pico_timeframe: 182 people 60+ with frailty (mean age 74) having elective cancer surgery, Ottawa / home-based exercise plus nutrition guidance, mean 5 weeks / standard care plus written advice / 6-minute walk distance at first postoperative clinic visit.
claims.safe_wording: A Canadian trial of home exercise before cancer surgery in 182 older people with frailty found no clear difference in walking distance after surgery. People kept to about 6 in 10 of the planned exercise on average.
claims.qualifications: Published in Br J Anaesth 2022 (not JAMA Surg). The better results in people with 80% or more adherence come from a secondary analysis and may reflect who adheres; do not present as the main finding.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None beyond C02-24-f.

numbers.meaning: patients analysed (204 randomised)
mean age in years
mean adherence to the programme
difference in 6-minute walk distance, not statistically significant

claims.claim: Recent pooled analyses of prehabilitation in older and frail surgical patients disagree, and frail patients remain understudied.
claims.supporting_passage: Liu 2026: "Nine randomized controlled trials involving 1027 patients were included. The meta-analysis showed that prehabilitation significantly reduced the risk of postoperative complications (risk ratio [RR] = 0.67, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.46 to 0.99, p = 0.04), with low heterogeneity among studies (I² = 24%). Subgroup analyses indicated a greater trend towards risk reduction in frail patients (RR = 0.53, 95% CI: 0.24 to 1.16)" ... "the trend suggesting potentially greater benefit in specifically frail patients requires confirmation in future larger, specifically designed trials." Lopez-Gonzalez 2025: "Five studies involving 400 participants were included. The p-MD for the 6MWT showed no significant improvement at any time point" ... "The LOS was also not significantly reduced" ... "Prehabilitation did not significantly improve aerobic capacity or reduce hospital stay." Buckinx 2026: "Nine studies (n = 36–182; mean/median age 68–82) were included." ... "Vascular surgery studies showed modest reductions in complications and hospital stay, whereas abdominal surgery studies generally reported no significant improvements, except for isolated reductions in severe complications or gains in functional reserve." ... "Prehabilitation in older adults remains understudied, especially in frail patients, the oldest old, and cardiac surgery."
claims.pico_timeframe: Liu: 9 RCTs 2020 to 2025, patients 60+ or frail with gastrointestinal cancer, prehabilitation versus usual care, postoperative complications. Lopez-Gonzalez: 5 RCTs, 400 frail older surgical patients, walk test and length of stay. Buckinx: 9 RCTs in adults 65+, major abdominal, cardiac or vascular surgery.
claims.safe_wording: Newer reviews disagree. One pooled 9 trials in people aged 60 and over having bowel or stomach cancer surgery and found about a third fewer complications with prehabilitation (a relative figure), but the result for frail patients on their own was uncertain. Another pooled 5 trials in frail older people and found no clear improvement in walking or length of stay. A third concluded that prehabilitation for frail and very old people is still understudied.
claims.qualifications: Relative risk only; no absolute numbers are available from these abstracts, so do not give 'N in 100'. Liu's search began in 2020 and the overall result only just reached significance. Do not cite the retracted Xie 2025 meta-analysis (PMID 41518969).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: The direction of the evidence is genuinely unsettled; this is why the post should counsel uncertainty rather than state that prehabilitation does not work.

numbers.meaning: relative risk of complications with prehabilitation versus usual care, 9 RCTs, 1,027 patients aged 60+ or frail, gastrointestinal cancer surgery; about a third fewer in relative terms
frail subgroup in the same analysis; not statistically significant
Lopez-Gonzalez 2025 meta-analysis in frail older people; no significant change in walk distance or length of stay
Buckinx 2026 review of RCTs in adults 65+; programme lengths

candidates.reason: The 2007 review (full text read) supports preserved but below-normal implicit motor learning in Alzheimer's disease and recommends frequent, consistent practice in a realistic setting with the person's own equipment, avoiding dual tasks. Hauer 2012 RCT shows dementia-adapted training improved strength and chair-stand performance, and cognitive impairment did not predict response. The access gap is supported by Seitz 2016 (about 4 in 10 received no rehabilitation after hip fracture, Ontario), but not as 'exclusion because of dementia'. Limitations answered: laboratory tasks, Alzheimer's only, Palma 2023 counter-evidence. 'Show' and 'use few words' were not tested in Alzheimer's disease and must be framed as practical suggestions; the visual's two-memory diagram should say 'often relatively preserved', not 'intact'.

Baltes 1992 and 1994 support the described pattern and the staff-training result, but only from abstracts of small German studies published in the early 1990s (sample size and follow-up unknown). The angle's claim that doing tasks for people 'can cost ability later' is not supported as a finding (C02-14-g). Modern trials are mixed: Res-Care 2009 improved walking and bathing in 12 US nursing homes, while the 2024 Dutch SELF trial changed staff behaviour without a significant change in residents' self-reliance. The time-on-the-rota point is supported only as a staff-reported barrier (time pressure and staff shortages, SELF process evaluation 2026). Resnick citations are now verified.
candidates.revised_angle: Date the classic finding (Berlin researchers, published 1992 and 1994): help came when residents were dependent, and independent effort went unnoticed; training staff shifted this. Then show that it still applies: modern staff programmes change what staff do, with gains for residents in some trials (US, 12 homes: walking, bathing) and no clear change in others (Netherlands, 28 wards). Nurses in the Dutch trial named time pressure and staff shortages as why they still took over tasks. The position, marked as judgement: supported self-care needs time and training built into how care is organised, not only goodwill. No causal claim that helping causes loss of ability; no time figure on the visual clock.

candidates.reason: The wrist-crease height, the opposite-hand rule and the choice of frame versus stick are supported as professional advice (Bradley 2011 clinical review). How common the problems are is supported by an English clinic survey (Sheehan 2008: 44% wrong length, 54% poor condition mainly worn ferrule, 38% incorrect use) and the US Liu study (problems named, no percentages). The worn-ferrule claim now has an opened source (Sheehan), but 'grips less well' must not be stated as a finding. Follows the judge: lead with the wrist-crease check as a quick test; add when a stick is the wrong aid; say the opposite-hand rule is for one-sided problems; attribute 'often wrong' to the specific studies.

Carli 2020 is supported as described (110 frail patients, mean age 78, 4-week programme before versus the same programme after bowel cancer surgery, no clear difference in complications or walking recovery). But the wider evidence has moved: a 2026 meta-analysis of 9 trials in older gastrointestinal cancer patients found fewer complications (relative risk 0.67; frail subgroup uncertain), while a 2025 meta-analysis of 5 trials in frail older people found no clear gain in walking or stay, and a 2026 review calls frail patients understudied. The umbrella review certainty ratings are confirmed (low to very low for complications; moderate for functional recovery with any prehabilitation in cancer surgery, all adults). PREHAB is confirmed but was published in Br J Anaesth 2022. A 2025 'high certainty' meta-analysis (Xie, PMID 41518969) is retracted per Scite and must not be cited. The post should not imply prehabilitation does not work; the defensible position is not to promise fewer complications.
candidates.revised_angle: Reading the evidence: why frail older people should not be promised fewer complications from prehabilitation. The trial built for frail older people (Carli 2020) compared a 4-week programme before bowel cancer surgery with the same programme after it (per editor guidance) and found no clear difference in complications or walking recovery; a home-exercise trial (PREHAB 2022) found no clear difference in walking. Pooled reviews disagree and are low certainty for complications. Closing counselling sentence practitioners can use: offer prehabilitation for its possible benefits to fitness and recovery, and tell people it has not been shown reliably to prevent complications in frail older people. Category fit partly C07; keep the focus on exercise and function.
